itemListElement.name: How to Choose Welding Management Software

mainEntity.name: What should I look for in welding management software?

acceptedAnswer.text: Beyond the feature list, weigh the things that are hard to change later: whether it reduces work or just digitizes paperwork, how it maintains the qualification chain (WPS to WPQR/PQR to welder qualification) and the continuity clock the codes require, how far it reaches into downstream inspection (NDT) and PWHT, where your records live, and whether the price is published. Score every tool on the same questions rather than counting features.

mainEntity.name: How do I know a tool will actually hold up in an audit?

acceptedAnswer.text: Ask to see it produce evidence, not store it. A tool passes the audit test when any weld can be traced — in one pull — to its material heat number, the WPS and qualification record behind it (WPS to WPQR/PQR, per ISO 15614 / ASME IX), the qualified welder, and the inspection result, with a clear history of any change. If assembling that for an auditor means exporting from several places and stitching it by hand, the tool is a filing cabinet, not audit-ready. Ask the vendor to walk one joint end to end in a demo.

mainEntity.name: How is welder qualification and continuity tracked?

acceptedAnswer.text: A welder's qualification (ISO 9606, or performance qualification under ASME IX) certifies them for a range of work, and most codes require ongoing continuity — evidence they have kept welding within that range, commonly on a six-month interval under ISO 9606. Capable software derives continuity from real production entries and warns before a qualification lapses, rather than leaving it to a spreadsheet of expiry dates.

mainEntity.name: Should welding software handle NDT and PWHT?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on your work. Non-destructive testing (visual, RT, UT, MT, PT) and post-weld heat treatment carry records a code auditor expects tied to the joint — heavily so for pressure work under ASME, less so for light structural work under EN 1090. Decide which downstream records your code actually demands, then ask each vendor precisely how far their coverage goes rather than accepting a blanket yes.

mainEntity.name: Is on-premise or cloud better for welding records?

acceptedAnswer.text: Neither is universally better; they trade off differently. Cloud is convenient and needs no hardware, but your records sit on shared infrastructure and the bill often scales per seat. On-premise keeps records on hardware you own with more predictable cost and stronger data control, at the price of owning an appliance. For shops weighing audits, cost and continuity, ownership often wins.

mainEntity.name: How does Elenchon fit into this?

acceptedAnswer.text: Elenchon is the on-premise archetype: a self-hosted appliance that runs the full WPS/WPQR/WPQ workflow, weld traceability, equipment and consumables in one system, with pricing published in the open and a zero-trust security layer. It is built so the software does the work rather than digitizing paperwork.
